instruction.what: Step 3.1, the elements of one subgroup (stage 4, C1; the end of the loop for the subgroup): what the evidence of the subgroup shows of the elements of a behaviour of the inner being. The input is the evidence observations of the subgroup by marker (`to_take_up`, the senses first, then the 2.1 findings and the older evidence), not the verses; the verses are kept for an occasional read-back. A finding is a building block, never a claim about the behaviour as a whole (that is stage 5).
read: Read the observations to take up, in order: the senses (1.1) and their enrichments (1.2) first, then the 2.1 findings (pairings, qualifiers, entities, direction, double meanings), then the older evidence. The inner-being workings work more with the senses than with the surfaces, so findings rest on the senses first.

For each item a finding may use (`uses`): what is done and its mode (operation, with its chain), whether a refusal or a pursuit (polarity), what it is directed at (object), the outward act (enactment), the other party with the route (party), the circumstance, and what a qualifier or a variation of the word gives the working (role, the dimension). Never the meaning of the word (stage 1).

Read the older inner-being observations (`older_inner_being`) with them: each is considered first, accepted with a trace to evidence, restated where it says more than the evidence, consumed where a finding says the same, merged, or deleted where it cannot be made true.
Go back to a verse (`verses`) only where the evidence does not settle the question, and say why.
write: Fill `answer.findings`: each one observation, with a `key` unique in the answer, `kind` (of the item's kinds), `text`, `basis` (stated or read), `parts` with `item` (one of `uses`) and what the item needs (with `grounds`), and `nodes`: a `traced` node on each observation it rests on (from `to_take_up` or `may_rest_on_besides`) and an `occurrence` node, with its `role` chosen from the verse (characteristic, qualifier, object, relational target, enactment or standalone), on the occurrences those observations cover.
An occurrence outside the observations a finding rests on is allowed only with a `read_back` entry on the finding: {verse: the osis id, why}.
`not_used`: {observation id: reason} for every observation to take up that no finding rests on. Every one is rested on or declared, never both.

`older`: answer, once, each older inner-being observation (`older_inner_being`) that has a node on an occurrence your findings name (RW-13; the record lists any it misses, and refuses an answer to one on no named occurrence: those are shown, not demanded, IB-05): keep (with nature inner_being: it stands, traced to evidence), restate, merge, consume (carriers ["this"] or ids, mapping), delete_neither, or defer (collection, nature, finding).
`existing`: answer every earlier reading (`earlier_readings`: inner being of an earlier grouping on these occurrences) with accept, modify, delete, merge or leave, and its reason.
The text says what the evidence shows of the element; it names its verses; it never restates a verse and never states the behaviour as a whole.

In place of writing `nodes`, a finding may name `rests_on` (the observations it rests on) and `role` (the node role of the words they cover; `roles` {occurrence: role, or "" to leave one out} for the exceptions): the recorder writes a traced node on each and an occurrence node on each occurrence they cover (each observation's `covers` or `occurrences` lists them). Nodes written by hand are kept.

Then: Collection-Build.ps1 -Action CheckAnswer -File <the answer file>: every problem at once, each with its rule, nothing written; correct the answer until it finds none, then -Action RecordElements -File <the answer file>. The record refuses the whole file on any fault and lists every fault.

keep.text: Stage 4 starts from the observations, not the verses (researcher, #2526 Q7, 2026-11-21): the subgroups and the stage 3 observations on them are the input, the behaviours are discovered from analysing them, and the base data is read back into only occasionally. Every finding of step 3.1 or 3.2 rests on named observations (a traced node on each, with an occurrence node as well) and its occurrence nodes lie within the occurrences those observations cover; an occurrence outside them is allowed only where the finding records a read-back (the verse and why). Each node has a role from reading.node_roles other than lexical, chosen by the reading. A 3.3 finding carries nodes on the occurrences of both sides in the shared verses. In 3.1 a qualification finding may also hold, with the role qualifier, the occurrences of the partner words the subgroup's 2.1 qualifier observations name, where the reading judges the qualifier bears on the working; a qualifier that does not bear on it is declared in not_used with its reason, never forced into a finding.

A finding of a stage 4 row is checked by the rules of observationrecord.check and check_item_parts (kind, text, basis, route, parts.item and what the item needs, node roles, collection of each node) and by RG, RW and RS, which are not restated here: one observation for each finding, never a duplicate, with a node on each word it applies to (RO11, RW-03); founded in the observations and never a restatement of the verse (B:131); parts.item is one of the items the row's item uses (cfg_setting layer.reading). An observation whose nodes all bear on an act is refused: those words are nodes of the observation of the act. A finding is a building block of a behaviour and never a claim (stage 5).

Nothing the step reads is lost on the way to stage 5. Step 3.1: every stage 3 observation of the subgroup is rested on by a finding or declared in not_used with its reason in words. Step 3.2: every 3.1 observation of the collection is gathered into a behaviour (a traced node on it from a flag finding of type discovery) or declared in not_gathered with its reason, and the row has at least one behaviour unless it is recorded as none with its reason. A behaviour names and gathers; it makes no claim about what the behaviour is.

An earlier inner-being observation with a node on the occurrences of a 3.1 row (any stage but those of the build: lexical, layer-1, layer-2, layer-3.1 to layer-3.3, and layer-3 before 2026-11-26) is shown in the pull for information and may be actioned in `existing`: accepted, modified, deleted, merged or left, each with its reason, through observationrecord (RW-01, RW-09); nothing is demanded of it, and it counts for nothing in the check. A row answered again withdraws its earlier observations with the reason. Every older live observation with a node on an occurrence of the row is answered in fill.older at the record of the row (RW-13); this rule's `existing` actions of stage 4 are unchanged.

Every live observation marked inner_being holds at least one live traced node on a live observation marked evidence, or on a live inner-being observation that itself traces to evidence (the trace chain of stage 4: a 3.2 behaviour traces the 3.1 elements it gathers, a 3.3 match the 3.1 and 3.2 observations it comes from; at most three links), unless it is recorded self-evidencing: it quotes its verse in full and holds a word node for every word it relies on. A traced node never points at a deleted observation. A trace points first at existing evidence; an evidence observation is created only when none states the fact and it states what the nodes and the quotation do not. An inner-being observation traced to evidence not yet marked is pending, not failed.

Find the main inner-being operation, and give every word that bears on it its role in this finding (cfg_setting reading.node_roles): characteristic, qualifier and what it gives the characteristic, object or content, relational target, or enactment. A word read in the verse that holds nothing for the inner being is standalone. The role comes from this verse, never from the cluster tag. Where a standalone word proves to qualify a characteristic, it is a qualifier of it.

A qualifier gets no separate account of itself, but what it gives the characteristic it binds to is evaluated for its value and recorded as a qualification finding, applied by its nodes to the qualifier (role qualifier) and the characteristic (role characteristic). What it gives can vary widely: grade, nature, impact, size, relation, a measure, strengthening, ground, cause, object, setting or bait are examples, not a list (#2273 D9). A qualifier whose usage varies across contexts may earn its own reading later.

Record the parties: who bears the act, who causes it, who is acted on (source, target, impact, purpose), and the route (cfg_enum observation_route), whose meaning is cfg_behaviour_rule 72 (route-verses-hib-other-beings-data-only): A another being in its own right, B another being with the human inner being, C no bearing, data only; a verse may take A and B. A non-human being is never itself a HIB; a collective stays one HIB; an implied party is named as referential, never asserted.
Never close a verse or item on 'not X'. A role label is never a verdict; the close records what the verse is. Silence about the inner being is a finding, recorded as data with its reason.
A phenomenon hidden behind a stated or refrained act may be named, with the verb, clause or stated silence that grounds it, and whether it is stated or read.
Keep the source of an interior state apart from the source of an enablement to act.

A tagged word that works adverbially in an occurrence (a noun with a preposition qualifying the predicate, as 'in the counsel of the wicked') is a qualifier there, not the verse's characteristic. The role is per occurrence: the same word may be the characteristic elsewhere.
In a simile, the predicates of the vehicle (the tree that yields, does not wither) are read for what they say of the one compared (the tenor), not as the vehicle's own acts.
One observation per finding, never a duplicate description; a finding applying to several verses or words carries several nodes, each with the word's role in it.
One observation per finding: the same description is never written twice. Applied to another verse, word or scope it gains a node on the existing observation.
Observation text is concise and tied to this verse's content, never a restatement of the word's dictionary sense. A transliteration is never given without its gloss.

An observation is created with its marker (ib_observation.nature, from the item answered, cfg_setting layer.reading items.<item>.nature; a finding file never sets it) and every word node with the columns of layer.reading node_required. A column the data cannot give (layer.reading node_gap_columns: an empty morph in the source row, a surface with no placement in the collection index) is left empty and its reason is kept on the node (disposition_note); any other missing column refuses the whole file and nothing is written. A trace to a deleted observation is refused (IB-07).

Evidence states what the data are or show, tied to a verse. Inner being states how something works in the inner being, based on evidence, a building block of the stage 5 claims. The marker (ib_observation.nature) follows the content and purpose of the observation, never its stage (RS-04): an observation of any stage may be inner being when it traces to evidence. One that states both is split. The marker is set when the observation is created, by the item that is answered (cfg_setting layer.reading items.<item>.nature); a finding file never sets it; the validation changes it only where the content shows the item's nature does not hold.

The study's primary focus is the human inner being (HIB). Each verse read is routed by what it shows, and the route is recorded in its observation. (A) Other beings in their own right: a word used of God, angels, other spirits or nature (non-HIB) is routed to Ch 13 "Other beings" (13.1 Divine, 13.2 Angels, 13.3 Other spirits, 13.4 Nature), read for what the verses say that being is and does; for God, also how his character passed to the HIB through creation in his image, held open (#1984). (B) Another being interacting with the HIB is fully in HIB scope. A verse may take A and B, described from different angles. (C) A verse with no inner-being and no other-being bearing is still assessed and recorded as data, and does not enter the narrative.

A node is on one occurrence (verse_lexical_id) and carries the collection of its surface (a supportive node, the collection of the surface it supports); a node already on the observation for the same occurrence is not written twice, and takes the role. A node with no collection to carry, or on a verse out of scope (B:130), is not written and is listed.

LayerCheck validates a stage 4 row from the tables alone: the demanded occurrences and the observations the row may rest on are re-derived; at least one live observation of the stage of its step (layer-3.1, layer-3.2 or layer-3.3) with its stable_key on the row; each observation's parts still valid and its item one the row uses; each live node has a valid role, a collection and its subgroup; each observation has a traced node on an observation the row may rest on; in 3.1 and 3.2 each occurrence node lies in the occurrences of the observations it rests on or its verse is in the recorded read-back; the completeness of IB-04 (not_used, not_gathered, the behaviour of 3.2); no observation restates a run of the verse longer than reading.observation_items max_verse_words_copied. A row that fails is unvalidated and its step is not closed.

A behaviour (step 3.2) is one working of the inner being: one core operation, who or what does what, shown by several element observations of 3.1. Elements that show the same operation belong to one behaviour, whatever their mode, polarity, object, party or circumstance, and in whatever subgroup they sit; those differences are written as relating findings (operation, chain, party, circumstance, role). Different operations linked in sequence are a chain between behaviours, not one behaviour. A group that holds two operations is split; two groups that hold one operation are joined. An element that shows no working of a human inner being (another being in its own right, route A of B:72; a word that is not an act of the mind) is declared not gathered with its reason. A behaviour is named by what is done, never by what it means for the inner being (stage 5).

A step of the layered reading opens only when the grouping is finished (every surface placed in a subgroup or isolated with its reason, every subgroup holding a surface) and the previous step is closed; with -Subgroup the needs and gates are judged for that subgroup alone (#2538). Step S1 is read after the grouping; step 1.1 needs step S1 closed: every word of the subgroup (surface and lettered Strong's code) answered and validated. Opening derives one ledger row for each aspect the data demands (cfg_setting layer.reading); an aspect the data no longer demands is retired, a new one is added, and a second open changes nothing.

The nodes of a layer observation are the occurrences the aspect demands (a word's occurrences, the group's occurrences, the partner's occurrences in the verses they share), written by the recorder with the collection and the subgroup of each surface; they are never typed. An item answered by senses (word-sense) names, for each sense, the occurrences it holds for, and together the senses cover every occurrence; the recorder checks them against the data. The interpretation is the observation text, founded in what the evidence shows (basis stated or read, B:131) and tied to its verses (the text names them and does not restate them): the items of every step (S1, 1.1, 1.2, 2.1) state what the dictionary, the verses and the stored structure show of a word and never what a word does for the inner being; their nodes carry the role lexical and no route. The whole file is checked and written in one transaction; any problem refuses all of it. A row answered again withdraws its earlier observations with the reason.

An aspect is recorded as none only where its item allows it (cfg_setting layer.reading none_allowed) and with its reason in words. A group definition and a group's Strong's enrichment are always observed.

A read or record command names a live collection, a live subgroup of it where the read is by subgroup, and a step or item the layered reading knows. A command that names one that does not exist is refused and writes nothing.

An answer is the output form its read wrote: the `command` of that read; every entry an object, or a list, where the form has one; each field in its place with its type (a key unique in the answer, a text, a reason in words); each item answered once; and at least one entry where the form asks for entries. A file in another shape is refused whole and nothing is written.

Every ledger row, occurrence, observation, sense, node, verse and collection an answer names is one the packet offered for this unit, or a key the answer itself defines, and is live in the database. A name outside them is refused.

Every coded value of an answer (kind, basis, item, part, role, route, mode, polarity, flag type, disposition, verdict, action, nature, stage, status) is one of the values the configuration allows for it (cfg_enum, cfg_setting layer.reading, reading.observation_items, validate.reading), as the packet lists them. Any other value is refused.

A read or record runs only where the ledger has its unit at that step: the row open, or answered and not yet validated, and the steps before it closed (S1 before 1.1; the 2.1 rows before the sweep; the sweep before the evidence validation; its gate before 3.1; every subgroup through 3.1 before 3.2). Out of order it is refused, and the message names what comes first.

A read writes its packet within the time and size the configuration sets (cfg_setting layer.read_types: limits, package_max_chars, read_max_seconds). A read that would exceed them is refused, nothing is written, and the limit is named.

The code of the reading runs only where the configuration it reads is in place (the settings, steps, items, natures, enums and rules it names). Where the code is ahead of the configuration, the command is refused and names what is missing.

When a verse is worked, every existing observation and node on it, of any stage, is checked against the verse by its wording. The stage is not an indication of the nature of an observation and is never used to filter. Each observation is accepted, modified (changed in place; the old value, the new value and the reason are kept in ib_observation_change), soft deleted (the `deleted` column, with the reason), merged (a duplicate description, into the observation that is kept) or, when its wording shows it is not verse understanding, left exactly as it is with the reason. The check's fixes are part of it and need no separate approval. Nothing is physically deleted.
No observation is changed except by a reading, and every change is recorded with its reason. An observation no longer supported by the verse is soft-deleted, with the reason.

Every older live observation with a live node on an occurrence of the row (a stage that is not the build's own) is answered in fill.older when the row is recorded, once: keep or restate (each with its marker), merge into a named observation, consume (live observations carry its meaning, stated in words, verified before it is deleted), delete as neither (comment first), or defer to a named collection (marked now; only the finding is left to that collection). An observation already marked by the validation, answered in a build or deferred is not asked again. A new observation whose text equals that of another live observation of the collection is refused, the other named. LayerCheck re-derives both from the tables. The end state of a collection's build is that every observation of its scope is marked and fixed or deleted, every word node complete or with its reason, and each deferral owned by a named collection.

A lookup of related data in the build or the validation is by an indexed column and takes a chunk of ids (cfg_setting layer.scan chunk); none runs once for each item of a list, and a statement that uses more work than layer.scan max_vm_ops is stopped and named, nothing written (lib/scanguard.py). The tests refuse a statement of the build whose query plan scans a table (layer.scan scan_ok lists the temporary tables a statement may scan).

An older observation is deleted as consumed only when live observations carry its meaning: every word occurrence of it is on a live node of a carrier or named as not carried with its reason, the mapping is stated in words (what the old says, which carrier states each part), the traces to it are re-pointed or replaced, and the consumption is kept as `consumed_by`. An observation that holds more than one finding is split first.

An observation that is neither evidence nor inner being contributes nothing to the purposes of the observations (researcher, 2026-11-22): it is commented with its reason and the word occurrences no other live observation holds, then deleted. An observation already marked, or one another observation traces, is not deleted this way.

asks: What do the stage 3 observations of this subgroup (its definition, its Strong's enrichment, its pairings, qualifiers, entities, direction, relations and double meanings, with the stage 1 senses) show of the elements of a behaviour of the inner being: what is done and its mode, whether a refusal or a pursuit, what it is directed at, the outward act, the other party with the route, the circumstance, the chain of operations, and the dimensions of the working (what a qualifier or a variation of the word gives it, from the lexical variation the stage 3 observations record)? Each finding is one observation that rests on named observations (a traced node on each) and carries nodes on the occurrences those observations cover, with the role each has; an occurrence outside them is allowed only with a read-back (the verse and why). Every stage 3 observation of the subgroup is rested on by a finding or declared not used, with the reason. A finding is a building block and never a claim about the behaviour as a whole (stage 5).

G0075.meaning_range: to fight, struggle, often an athletic contest; to be a combatant in the public games; to contend, fight, strive earnestly

G1377.meaning_range: to pursue, persecute, to systematically oppress and harass a person or group, as an extended meaning of pursuing a person on foot in a chase; also from the image of the chase comes the meaning of striving and pressing on to a goal with intensity: to press on; to put in rapid motion; to pursue; to follow, pursue the direction of, Lk. 17:23; to follow eagerly, endeavor earnestly to acquire, Rom. 9:30, 31; 12:13; to press forw

G4704.meaning_range: to be eager, make every effort, do one’s best; to hurry; be bent upon, Gal. 2:10; to endeavor earnestly, strive, make every effort, to do one’s best Eph. 4:3

H1624.meaning_range: 1) to cause strife, stir up, contend, meddle, strive, be stirred up; 1a) (Piel) to stir up strife, excite strife; 1b) (Hithpael); 1b1) to excite oneself against, engage in strife; 1b2) to excite oneself (against foe), wage war

H7379.meaning_range: 1) strife, controversy, dispute; 1a) strife, quarrel; 1b) dispute, controversy, case at law

to_take_up.text: Exertion toward a goal: effort spent to reach or to do something, in 1Th 2:17, Gal 2:17, Luk 13:24, 1Ti 4:10, Heb 12:14, 1Cor 14:12, Heb 4:11 and Ecc 2:22; the goal is named in each, a meeting, a standing before God, entry, peace and holiness, excelling, rest, or in Ecc 2:22 the labour itself.

Contention against an opponent: disputing with another or rousing oneself against another, in Isa 45:9 against one's maker, in Pro 28:4 by those who keep the law against the wicked, and in Isa 41:11 where Israel's opponents are named by their dispute with Israel.
Physical fighting: a bodily fight between men in Exo 21:22 and warfare between peoples in Psa 60:1, both with the verb natsah.
Jacob's contending with God: the struggle with God, or with the angel, in which Jacob prevailed, told in Gen 32:28, Hos 12:3 and Hos 12:4 with sarah and sur.

A reaching after wind: in Ecc 1:14, Ecc 1:17, Ecc 2:11, Ecc 2:17, Ecc 2:26, Ecc 4:4, Ecc 4:6, Ecc 4:16 and Ecc 6:9 two related nouns, reut and rayon, name a striving after wind, a reaching after what gives nothing to hold.

Each code of this sense names effort toward a goal from its own side: spoudazo (G4704) eagerness and haste, agonizomai (G0075) struggle as in a contest, zeteo (G2212) seeking to obtain, dioko (G1377) pursuit pressed to a goal, and rayon (H7475) longing. The surface strive carries all four Greek codes, so Luk 13:24, Heb 12:14, 1Cor 14:12 and Heb 4:11 differ by code. The lexicon bears out the sense.

rib as verb (H7378) and noun (H7379) covers contending in words or at law and quarrel; garah (H1624) in its Hithpael is to rouse oneself against another and engage in strife. The lexicon bears out a contention against another in Isa 45:9, Isa 41:11 and Pro 28:4; the surface strive carries both the noun H7379 and the verb H1624.

natsah (H5327A) is given only as to struggle, in the Niphal of Exo 21:22 and the Hiphil of Psa 60:1; the lexicon gives no more than struggle, so the bodily and armed nature of the fight comes from the verses. H3588A (ki, that, when) is the conjunction the surface carries in Exo 21:22 and adds no meaning to the sense.

sarah (H8280) is to contend, persist and persevere, and its related words include Israel (H3478), the name Gen 32:28 explains. sur (H7786) has rule and reign as its head sense, but its range includes contend and prevail over, which Hos 12:4 uses. The lexicon bears out the sense for both codes, with sur lying nearer to ruling.

reut (H7469) and rayon (H7475) are given the same range, longing and striving, and their related words include words for thought (H7454, H7476) and for pasturing (H7462B). The lexicon bears out the sense of a reaching after in Ecc 1:14 and Ecc 1:17, and adds nothing on the wind it is joined with.
In Ecc 2:11 the Preacher considered all his work and toil and found it vanity and a striving after wind: the considering is a review of his toil that reaches its verdict.

In Exo 21:22 the surface strive stands on two codes at one position: natsah (H5327A, struggle, Niphal) and ki (H3588A, the conjunction 'when'), so the one English word holds both the opening conjunction and the verb of a fight between men.

In Pro 28:4 (garah, H1624, a Hithpael verb) and Isa 41:11 (rib, H7379, a noun in construct) the surface strive stands on two Hebrew codes of contention, each followed by the party opposed, 'them' and 'you'.

In Luk 13:24, 1Ti 4:10, 1Cor 14:12, Heb 4:11 and Heb 12:14 the surface strive stands on four Greek codes, agonizomai (G0075), zeteo (G2212), spoudazo (G4704) and dioko (G1377), each with a goal as an infinitive or an object: one English word covers struggle, seeking, eagerness and pursuit.

In Ecc 1:14, 2:11, 2:17, 2:26, 4:4, 4:6 and 6:9 (reut, H7469) and in Ecc 1:17 and 4:16 (rayon, H7475) the surface striving stands in the same construct phrase with 'wind', so the two codes give one face in that phrase.

In Ecc 2:22 striving stands on rayon (H7475) in construct with 'heart' and joined to 'toil', with no 'wind': the code that gives the phrase with wind in Ecc 1:17 and 4:16 here names the effort of the heart in labour.
In Psa 60:1 the surface strove stands on natsah (H5327A, a Hiphil infinitive) for David's warfare against Aram-naharaim and Aram-zobah, in the superscription.

In Hos 12:3 (sarah, H8280, with God) and Hos 12:4 (sur, H7786, with the angel) the surface strove stands on two different codes for the one struggle of Jacob, told in two lines that follow each other.

In 1Th 2:17 the comparative adverb 'more eagerly' (G4056) qualifies endeavored, and 'great' (G4183) qualifies 'desire', the noun of the phrase that goes with the verb; the negator 'not' (G3756) reaches 'in heart', set against 'in person', not the verb.

In Ecc 1:17, 2:26, 4:4, 4:16 and 6:9 the adverb 'also' (gam, H1571) stands in the clause that calls the case a striving after wind, adding it to the cases already called so; it reaches the clause, not the noun striving.

In Ecc 4:6 and 6:9 'better' (tov, H2896A) opens a comparison in which the striving after wind stands on the side judged the lesser: with two hands full of toil in 4:6, with the wandering of the appetite in 6:9.

In Ecc 2:17, 2:22 and 2:26 the adjectives grievous (H7451A), toils (H6001B) and pleases (H2896A) qualify other words of their verses, what is done under the sun, the man who labours, and the one who pleases God; none reaches striving.
In Gen 32:28 the negator 'no' with 'longer' (H3808, H5750) reaches 'be called Jacob', the old name, not the verb striven.
In Exo 21:22 'pregnant' (H2030A) qualifies the woman struck and 'no' (H3808) negates 'harm'; neither reaches strive.
In Hos 12:4 the adverb 'there' (H8033G) reaches 'spoke', placing God's speaking at Bethel; it does not reach strove.
In Luk 13:24 'narrow' (G4728) qualifies the door that is the goal of the striving; 'many' (G4183) names those who seek, and 'not' (G3756) negates 'be able' in their clause, not the command to strive.
In 1Cor 14:12 'so' (G3779) opens the sentence and applies what went before to the readers; it reaches the whole sentence and not strive alone.
In Gal 2:17 'sinners' (G0268) is what those who endeavor are found to be, and 'not' (G3361) closes the verse as a denial of the question about Christ; neither reaches the endeavor.
In 1Ti 4:10 'all' (G3956), 'especially' (G3122) and 'believe' (G4103) qualify the people of whom God is Savior, in the clause about him; none reaches strive.
In Heb 12:14 'everyone' (G3956) gives the range of the peace that is pursued, and 'no one' (G3762) is the subject of 'will see', in the clause about holiness.

In Gen 32:28 and Hos 12:3 the striving is with God (elohim, H0430G), and in Gen 32:28 also with men (H0582); the one who strove is Jacob (H3290), named in Gen 32:28 and referred to by 'he' in Hos 12:3.
In Exo 21:22 those who strive are 'men' (H0582), not named, and a third party, a pregnant woman (H0802G), is struck by them; her husband is named after, as the one who sets the fine.

In Psa 60:1 the one who strove is David (H1732), named in the superscription with Joab (H3097G) and the peoples fought; God (H0430G) is addressed in the body of the verse, not named as a party of the fighting.
In Ecc 2:22 and 2:26 the one who labours is 'a man' (adam, H0120G), in 2:26 set under God (H0430G), who gives to the one who pleases him; in Ecc 4:4 the neighbor (H7453) is the one envied.
In Isa 41:11 those who strive are 'those' (H0582, men in construct with the noun of strife), the opponents of the one addressed as 'you'.
In Gal 2:17 Christ (G5547) is named twice, as the one in whom justification is sought and as the subject of the question whether he serves sin.
In 1Th 2:17 the readers are addressed as 'brothers' (G0080), the ones from whom the writers were torn away and whom they made the effort to see.
In 1Ti 4:10 the living God (G2316) is the one on whom the hope of those who strive is set, and the Savior of all people (G0444); the strivers are 'we'.
In Heb 12:14 the Lord (G2962G) is the one who will not be seen without holiness; the strivers are the readers addressed by the imperative.
In Gen 32:28 and Hos 12:3 the striving goes from Jacob toward God, with the preposition 'with' (H5973A, H0854); in Gen 32:28 it also goes toward men, and the verse closes on his prevailing.
In Exo 21:22 the striving runs both ways between the men (Niphal, 'together'), and their blows fall on a third party, the pregnant woman they strike.
In Psa 60:1 the striving goes from David against two peoples, Aram-naharaim and Aram-zobah, while the body of the verse turns to God in address.
In Isa 41:11 the striving comes from opponents against the one addressed, 'against you'.
In 1Th 2:17 the effort goes from the writers toward persons, the brothers they want to see face to face.

In Gal 2:17, 1Ti 4:10 and Heb 12:14 the effort goes toward an end and against no party: justification in Christ, 'this end' with hope set on God, and peace with everyone with the holiness without which the Lord is not seen.

In Ecc 2:22, 2:26 and 4:4 the striving is directed at no party: it is a man's own labour in 2:22, the business God gives to the sinner in 2:26, and work that comes from a man's envy of his neighbor in 4:4.

In Psa 60:1 'angry' (anaph, H0599) is said of God toward his people in the prayer of the verse, while 'strove' stands in the superscription for David's wars; the two words lie in different parts of the verse.
In Isa 41:11 'incensed' (H2734) and 'those who strive against you' are two parallel names for the same opponents, each clause with its own outcome, shame and perishing.
In Ecc 6:9 'wandering' (H1980I, an infinitive) of the appetite stands on the lesser side of the comparison, and the same clause then calls it a striving after wind.
In 1Ti 4:10 'believe' (G4103) names those of whom God is especially Savior, in the clause that gives the ground of the toil and striving.
In Exo 21:22 'harm' (two codes, H0611 and H1961) is negated: the case set out is a fight that brings the birth but no further harm, which decides the penalty.
In Ecc 2:11 'gained' (yitron, H3504) follows the striving after wind and is negated: the toil under the sun is said to leave no gain.
In Gen 32:28 'called' (H0559, Niphal) gives the renaming of Jacob, and the clause with 'striven' is joined to it by 'for' as its reason.
In Pro 28:4 'praise' (H1984B) of the wicked by those who forsake the law is set opposite the striving against the wicked by those who keep it.
In Exo 21:22 'judges' (H6414) set the payment due after the fight between the men; the word stands at the close of the case, not with strive.
In Isa 41:11 'confounded' (H3637) is the outcome for the incensed, in the clause parallel to the one where those who strive against Israel come to nothing.

In Ecc 2:26 'pleases' (H2896A, H6440G) and 'joy' (H8057) belong to the one God favours, who receives wisdom, knowledge and joy, set against the sinner's business of gathering, which is called a striving after wind.
In Hos 12:4 'favor' (H2603A, Hithpael) follows the striving: after prevailing, Jacob wept and sought favor.
In Ecc 6:9 'appetite' (nephesh, H5315L) is the one whose wandering is set below the sight of the eyes and called a striving after wind.
In 1Cor 14:12 'eager' (zelotes, G2207) names the readers' eagerness for manifestations of the Spirit, and the imperative 'strive' that follows turns it to building up the church.
In 1Th 2:17 'desire' (epithymia, G1939) qualified by 'great' goes with endeavored in a prepositional phrase, naming what went with the effort to see the readers.
In Isa 41:11 'perish' (H0006) is the end of those who strive against Israel, after 'shall be as nothing'.
In Pro 28:4 'wicked' (H7563) are the ones the law-keepers strive against, referred to again by 'them' after the verb.
In Ecc 1:17 'madness' (H1947) and 'folly' (H5531A) are objects of 'to know', set beside wisdom; the applying of the heart to know them is what the verse calls a striving after wind.
In Pro 28:4 'forsake' (H5800A, a participle) names those who leave the law and praise the wicked, set opposite those who keep it and strive.
In Ecc 4:16 'rejoice' (H8055) is negated: those who come after take no joy in the one who led the people, and the verse then calls it a striving after wind.
In Heb 12:14 'holiness' (hagiasmos, G0038) is the second object of 'strive for', after peace, and the clause after it makes it the condition of seeing the Lord.

In Ecc 4:16 'led' (three codes, H6440G, H0834A, H1961: those he was before) names the people without end whom one man led; the lack of joy in him among those who come later is called a striving after wind.
In Ecc 1:17 'heart' (lev, H3820A) is the object of 'applied': the speaker applied his heart to know, and that knowing is then called a striving after wind.
In Ecc 2:22 'heart' (lev, H3820A) stands in construct after striving, so the striving is of the heart, joined to the toil.
In 1Th 2:17 'heart' (kardia, G2588) stands in the contrast 'in person, not in heart', which comes just before endeavored.
In Isa 41:11 'put to shame' (H0954) is the outcome for the incensed, in the clause parallel to the one where those who strive against Israel come to nothing.
In 1Ti 4:10 'hope' (G1679, a perfect: hope set and standing) gives the ground of the toil and striving, in the clause after 'because'.

In Ecc 4:4 'envy' (qinah, H7068, with H3588A and H1931 at the same place) of a man toward his neighbor is named as the source of all toil and skill in work, which the verse then calls a striving after wind.
In Ecc 1:17 'know' (yada, H3045) is used three times: twice for setting the heart to know wisdom, madness and folly, and once for perceiving that this too is a striving after wind.
In Ecc 2:26 'knowledge' (H1847) is one of the gifts God gives to the one who pleases him, set against the sinner's business that is called a striving after wind.

In Ecc 2:11, 2:22, 4:4 and 4:6 'toil' (amal, H5999), and in 4:4 also 'work' (H4639G), stand with striving in one verse: joined to it by 'and' in 2:22 and 4:6, and in 2:11 and 4:4 as what the verse then calls a striving after wind.
In Isa 45:9 'work' (H6467) is the potter's work in the clay's mouth, a complaint that it has no handles, which pictures the one who strives with his maker.
In 1Ti 4:10 'toil' (kopiao, G2872) is paired with strive by 'and', both verbs of the same subject and with the same end.
In Ecc 2:17 'grievous' (H7451A) says how what is done under the sun weighed on the speaker; it gives the reason he hated life, before the verse calls it all a striving after wind.
In Hos 12:4 'wept' (H1058) follows strove and prevailed: after the struggle Jacob wept and sought favor.
In 1Ti 4:10 'living' (G2198, a participle) describes God, the one on whom the hope behind the striving is set.
In Ecc 2:17 'hated' (H8130) has life as its object and opens the verse; the reason follows, and the verse ends by calling it all a striving after wind.
In Exo 21:22 'surely' (H6064, an infinitive absolute) doubles the verb 'fined', making the penalty after the fight certain.
In Ecc 4:16 'surely' (ki, H3588A) opens the closing clause with emphasis, the clause that calls it a striving after wind.
In Ecc 4:6 'quietness' (H5183A) is on the side judged better, a single handful of it set against two hands full of toil and striving after wind.
In Heb 4:11 'rest' (katapausis, G2663) is the goal of strive, the rest the hearers are urged to enter.
In Gen 32:28 and Hos 12:4 'prevailed' (H3201) follows the striving in both tellings and is joined to it by 'and', so the struggle is told with its outcome.

In Ecc 1:14, 2:11, 2:17, 2:26, 4:4, 4:16 and 6:9 'vanity' (hevel, H1892) is joined to striving by 'and' as the first of the two names given to the case; in 4:16 'this' (H2088) stands at the same place.
In Heb 12:14 'peace' (eirene, G1515) is the first object of strive for, its range given by 'with everyone'.
In Psa 60:1 'restore' (H7725H) is the plea that closes the prayer of the verse, apart from the superscription where 'strove' stands.
In Psa 60:1 'rejected' (H2186A) is said of God toward his people in the prayer of the verse, apart from the superscription where 'strove' names David's wars.
In Pro 28:4 'keep' (shamar, H8104G, a participle) names the subject of strive: those who keep the law, set opposite those who forsake it.
In Psa 60:1 'return' (H7725G) is Joab's coming back from the wars, in the clause of the superscription that follows David's striving.
In Exo 21:22 'pay' (H5414N) is what the one who struck the woman must do after the fight, the amount set by the husband and the judges.
In Gal 2:17 'justified' (dikaioo, G1344, an aorist passive infinitive) is the goal of the endeavor, a standing received in Christ.
In Luk 13:24 'seek' (zeteo, G2212, future) is what the many will do to enter, set against the command to strive, and followed by their not being able.

In Ecc 2:26 'given' and 'give' (natan, H5414G) are used three times: God gives wisdom, knowledge and joy to the one who pleases him, gives the sinner the business of gathering, and that gathering is given on to the one who pleases God.
In Ecc 2:26 'sinner' (H2398, a participle) is the one given the business of gathering, the part of the verse called a striving after wind.
In Gal 2:17 'sinners' (G0268) is what those who endeavor are found to be, and 'sin' (G0266) stands in the question whether Christ is its servant.
In Ecc 4:4 'skill' (H3788) in work is named with toil as coming from envy, and both are then called a striving after wind.
In Luk 13:24 'able' (ischyo, G2480) is negated: the many who seek will lack the strength to enter, set against the command to strive.
In Heb 4:11 'disobedience' (G0543) stands in the purpose clause after strive: the effort is made so that no one falls by it.
In Psa 60:1 'instruction' (lamad, H3925G, an infinitive) gives the purpose of the psalm in its superscription, before the clause of David's striving.
In Ecc 2:11 'considered' (H6437G, turned to look) opens the verse: the speaker looks over his work and toil, and what he sees he calls a striving after wind.
In Isa 45:9 'woe' (hoy, H1945) opens the verse and is pronounced on the one who strives with his maker.
In Ecc 1:17 'wisdom' (H2451) is the first object of 'to know', set beside madness and folly, in the knowing the verse calls a striving after wind.
In Ecc 2:26 'wisdom' (H2451) is a gift of God to the one who pleases him, on the side set against the sinner's striving after wind.
Context Ecc 2:17–20: "So I hated life … a striving after wind" (17) → "I hated all my toil" (18) → "I … gave my heart up to despair" (20)
Heart present, body absent: "torn away from you … in person not in heart, we endeavored … with great desire to see you" (1Th 2:17).
Ecc 6:9 calls the wandering of the appetite (nephesh) vanity and a striving after wind, set after the sight of the eyes, which it says is better.
Ecc 4:4 traces all toil and skill in work to the envy a man has of his neighbour, and calls that too a striving after wind.
In 1Th 2:17-18 the eager effort to come back to the Thessalonians is said to have been blocked again and again, and the one who blocked it is named as Satan.

may_rest_on_besides.text: In 1Th 2:17 spoudazo (be eager, make every effort; aorist active, first plural) names the effort Paul and his companions made to see the Thessalonians again after being parted from them; the adverb 'the more eagerly' and the phrase 'with great desire' heighten it, and its goal is the infinitive 'to see you'.

In Gal 2:17 zeteo (seek, try to obtain; present active participle, plural) has the infinitive 'to be justified in Christ' as its goal, so the seeking is aimed at a standing before God rather than at finding a thing or person; the ESV renders the participle as the noun phrase 'our endeavor'.

In Gen 32:28 sarah (contend, persevere; Qal perfect, second masculine singular) names Jacob's contending with God and with men, a struggle he came through, since the verse joins it to 'and have prevailed'; the verb is given as the reason for the new name Israel.

In Isa 45:9 rib (contend, quarrel; Qal participle) names the one who disputes with his maker; the verse pictures it as clay questioning the potter about what he makes, so the striving here is a complaint raised against the one who formed him.

In Luk 13:24 agonizomai (struggle, contend as in a contest; present imperative, second plural) is a command to struggle to get in, its goal the infinitive 'to enter through the narrow door', set against the many who will only seek to enter and fail.

In 1Ti 4:10 agonizomai (struggle, labour hard; present indicative, first plural) stands paired with 'toil' for the ongoing labour of Paul and his fellow workers 'to this end', and the verse gives its ground in their hope set on the living God.

In Heb 12:14 dioko, whose usual sense is to chase or pursue a person, is a present imperative with the objects peace with everyone and holiness, rendered 'Strive for': the pursuit is of a state to be reached and held, not of a person, and the verse ties holiness to seeing the Lord.

In 1Cor 14:12 zeteo (seek, aim at; present active imperative, second plural) takes the infinitive 'to excel' with the goal of building up the church, and the verse sets it after the readers' eagerness for manifestations of the Spirit, directing that eagerness to a goal.

In Heb 4:11 spoudazo (be eager, make every effort; aorist subjunctive, first plural, a call to the hearers with the writer) has the goal 'to enter that rest', and the purpose clause sets it against falling by the same disobedience.

In Pro 28:4 garah (stir up strife; Hithpael imperfect, third masculine plural) is reflexive: those who keep the law rouse themselves against the wicked, set opposite those who forsake the law and praise them.

In Exo 21:22 natsah (struggle; Niphal imperfect, third masculine plural) is a physical fight between men, the Niphal with 'together' making it mutual, in a case of law where in the fight a pregnant woman is struck and gives birth early.

In Isa 41:11 rib is a noun in construct (strife, dispute) which the ESV renders as the verb phrase 'those who strive against you': the word names Israel's opponents by their quarrel with Israel, set beside those incensed against them, who will come to nothing.

In Ecc 1:14, 2:11, 2:17, 2:26, 4:4, 4:6 and 6:9 reut (longing, striving; a feminine noun in construct) is in each the phrase 'a striving after wind', set beside 'vanity' in six of them and beside 'toil' in 4:6: a reaching after what cannot be grasped, said of what is done under the sun.

In Ecc 1:17 and Ecc 4:16 rayon (longing, striving; a masculine noun in construct) is in the phrase 'a striving after wind', said in 1:17 of applying the heart to know wisdom, madness and folly, and in 4:16 of the people one man led, whom later generations take no joy in.

In Ecc 2:22 rayon is joined to 'heart' and paired with 'toil' ('the toil and striving of heart'): here it is the effort a man's heart spends in his labour beneath the sun, in a question asking what he has from it.

In Psa 60:1, in the superscription, natsah (struggle; Hiphil infinitive construct) names David's warfare against Aram-naharaim and Aram-zobah, set beside Joab's striking down of Edom: a fight between peoples, giving the occasion of the psalm.

In Hos 12:4 sur, whose head sense in the lexicon is to rule or act as prince, is a Qal narrative verb rendered 'strove' and used of Jacob contending with the angel and prevailing, the same event Hos 12:3 tells with sarah; here it is a struggle with a heavenly being, not a ruling.

In Hos 12:3 sarah (contend; Qal perfect, third masculine singular) names Jacob's contending with God in his manhood, set after his taking his brother by the heel in the womb; it recalls the struggle Gen 32:28 gives as the reason for the name Israel.

older_inner_being.text: "Vanity and a striving after wind" (*hevel* + *rûaḥ*): Ecc 1:14; 2:11, 17, 26; 4:4, 16; 6:9.
1.9 ◆ Desire aimed at wind: "all is vanity and a striving after wind" (Ecc 1:14; 2:11, 17, 26; 4:4, 6)

e. Wind and breath in relation to the inner being — explicitly retained per the researcher: *Breath = life in flesh:*; "all flesh in which is the breath of life" (Gen 6:17; 7:15, 22); "sinews … flesh … skin … But there was no breath in them" → "breath came into them, and they lived" (Eze 37:6–10); "When you take away their breath, they die and return to their dust" (Psa 104:29); *Breath and thought:* "When his breath departs, he returns to the earth; on that very day his plans perish" (Psa 146:4). Link to the thought vocabulary (see brief §5).; *Breath as frailty:* "Remember that my life is a breath" (Job 7:7); "They all have the same breath, and man has no advantage over the beasts" (Ecc 3:19); "He remembered that they were but flesh, a wind that passes and comes not again" (Psa 78:39).; *No breath = no inner life:* idols have "no breath in them" (Jer 10:14; 51:17; Hab 2:19; Psa 135:17). fringe: "there was no more breath in her" = the queen of Sheba overwhelmed (1Ki 10:5; 2Ch 9:4).; *Wind as the emptiness of inner striving* (Ecclesiastes): "I applied my heart to know wisdom … this also is but a striving after wind" (Ecc 1:17); the same in 1:14; 2:11, 17, 26; 4:4, 6, 16; 5:16; "Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the appetite: this also is vanity and a striving after wind" (Ecc 6:9) — appetite (nephesh) + wind; *Wind as empty words:*; "windy knowledge … fill his belly with the east wind" (Job 15:2); "windy words" (Job 16:3); "the speech of a despairing man is wind" (Job 6:26); "the words of your mouth be a great wind" (Job 8:2); "The prophets will become wind; the word is not in them" (Jer 5:13); "utter wind and lies" (Mic 2:11); *Wind as empty outcome:* "we have given birth to wind" (Isa 26:18); "Whoever troubles his own household will inherit the wind" (Pro 11:29); "sow the wind, and … reap the whirlwind" (Hos 8:7); "Ephraim feeds on the wind" (Hos 12:1).; *Wind as the image for a shaken heart:* "the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind" (Isa 7:2).; *Wind and lust:* "a wild donkey … in her heat sniffing the wind! Who can restrain her lust?" (Jer 2:24); "to restrain her is to restrain the wind" (Pro 27:16).

Seeking/striving here is the drive that channels eagerness (M18, zeal for spiritual gifts, M47 Spirit) into concrete edification (building up, M52) of the church (M44); from seeking's vantage, it is the pivot converting inward zeal into outward communal benefit -- first relational pass for this verse.

verses.text: So with yourselves, since you are eager for manifestations of the Spirit, strive to excel in building up the church.
But since we were torn away from you, brothers, for a short time, in person not in heart, we endeavored the more eagerly and with great desire to see you face to face,
For to this end we toil and strive, because we have our hope set on the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe.
I have seen everything that is done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and a striving after wind.
And I applied my heart to know wisdom and to know madness and folly. I perceived that this also is but a striving after wind.
Then I considered all that my hands had done and the toil I had expended in doing it, and behold, all was vanity and a striving after wind, and there was nothing to be gained under the sun.
So I hated life, because what is done under the sun was grievous to me, for all is vanity and a striving after wind.
What has a man from all the toil and striving of heart with which he toils beneath the sun?

For to the one who pleases him God has given wisdom and knowledge and joy, but to the sinner he has given the business of gathering and collecting, only to give to one who pleases God. This also is vanity and a striving after wind.
There was no end of all the people, all of whom he led. Yet those who come later will not rejoice in him. Surely this also is vanity and a striving after wind.
Then I saw that all toil and all skill in work come from a man’s envy of his neighbor. This also is vanity and a striving after wind.
Better is a handful of quietness than two hands full of toil and a striving after wind.
Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the appetite: this also is vanity and a striving after wind.

“When men strive together and hit a pregnant woman, so that her children come out, but there is no harm, the one who hit her shall surely be fined, as the woman’s husband shall impose on him, and he shall pay as the judges determine.
But if, in our endeavor to be justified in Christ, we too were found to be sinners, is Christ then a servant of sin? Certainly not!
Then he said, “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel, for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed.”
Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord.
Let us therefore strive to enter that rest, so that no one may fall by the same sort of disobedience.
In the womb he took his brother by the heel, and in his manhood he strove with God.
He strove with the angel and prevailed; he wept and sought his favor. He met God at Bethel, and there God spoke with us —
Behold, all who are incensed against you shall be put to shame and confounded; those who strive against you shall be as nothing and shall perish.
“ Woe to him who strives with him who formed him, a pot among earthen pots! Does the clay say to him who forms it, ‘ What are you making?’ or ‘Your work has no handles ’?
“ Strive to enter through the narrow door. For many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able.
Those who forsake the law praise the wicked, but those who keep the law strive against them.

To the choirmaster: according to Shushan Eduth. A Miktam of David; for instruction; when he strove with Aram-naharaim and with Aram-zobah, and when Joab on his return struck down twelve thousand of Edom in the Valley of Salt. O God, you have rejected us, broken our defenses; you have been angry; oh, restore us.

findings.text: In Luk 13:24, Heb 4:11, Heb 12:14 and 1Cor 14:12 the hearers are called to put effort toward a goal: entry through the narrow door, entry into rest, peace and holiness, and excelling in building up the church.

parts.grounds: Strive to enter through the narrow door

findings.text: In 1Th 2:17, 1Ti 4:10 and Gal 2:17 the writers report effort they themselves made toward a goal: to see the readers again, the end their labour serves, and being justified in Christ.

parts.grounds: we toil and strive

findings.text: In the verses of exertion toward a goal the act is a pursuit, never a refusal: each names something to be reached, an entry, a meeting, a standing, a state or a work, as 1Th 2:17, Luk 13:24 and Heb 12:14 show.

parts.grounds: Strive for peace with everyone

findings.text: The goal of the effort differs by verse: an entry (Luk 13:24, Heb 4:11), a state to hold, peace and holiness (Heb 12:14), a standing before God (Gal 2:17), persons to meet (1Th 2:17), a work for others (1Cor 14:12).

parts.grounds: strive to enter that rest

findings.text: In 1Th 2:17 the comparative 'more eagerly' grades the effort and 'great desire' goes with it: the effort is heightened and joined to a longing to see the readers.

parts.grounds: the more eagerly and with great desire

findings.text: In 1Ti 4:10 the toil and striving stand on a ground the verse gives after 'because': their hope, set and standing, rests on God, named as living and as Savior of all people.

parts.grounds: because we have our hope set on the living God

findings.text: In 1Cor 14:12 the readers' eagerness for manifestations of the Spirit comes first, and the command to strive turns it toward excelling in building up the church.

parts.grounds: since you are eager for manifestations of the Spirit

findings.text: In Luk 13:24 and Heb 4:11 the effort is set against a failure the verse names: many who seek to enter and are not able, and falling by the same disobedience.

parts.grounds: will seek to enter and will not be able

findings.text: In Ecc 2:22 the striving is of the heart, joined to toil under the sun, and the verse asks what a man has from it.

parts.grounds: striving of heart

findings.text: In 1Th 2:17 the effort to see the readers comes from writers absent in person but not in heart, addressed to them as brothers, and in 1Th 2:18 it was blocked by Satan.

parts.grounds: in person not in heart

findings.text: In Gal 2:17 those who seek to be justified in Christ are found to be sinners, and the verse asks whether Christ then serves sin, and denies it.

parts.grounds: we too were found to be sinners

findings.text: In Isa 45:9, Pro 28:4 and Isa 41:11 a person or party sets himself against another: one disputes with his maker, the law-keepers rouse themselves against the wicked, opponents quarrel with the one addressed.

parts.grounds: those who keep the law strive against them

findings.text: The one opposed differs: the one who formed the striver (Isa 45:9), the wicked (Pro 28:4), and the one addressed, Israel (Isa 41:11).

parts.grounds: strives with him who formed him

findings.text: In Isa 45:9 the other party of the dispute is the maker of the one who strives, pictured as the potter questioned by the clay, and a woe is pronounced on the striver.

parts.grounds: Woe to him who strives with him who formed him

findings.text: In Pro 28:4 striving against the wicked is what keeping the law looks like, set opposite the praise of the wicked by those who forsake the law.

parts.grounds: Those who forsake the law praise the wicked

findings.text: In Isa 41:11 those who strive against Israel come to nothing and perish, in parallel with the incensed, who are put to shame and confounded.

parts.grounds: shall be as nothing and shall perish

findings.text: In Exo 21:22 men fight one another and in Psa 60:1 David wars against two peoples: here the striving is bodily or armed fighting between parties, and neither verse states an inner act with it.

parts.grounds: When men strive together and hit a pregnant woman

findings.text: In Exo 21:22 the fight issues in a blow on a pregnant woman with no further harm, and the law sets a fine, certain to be paid as the judges determine.

parts.grounds: he shall pay as the judges determine

findings.text: In Gen 32:28, Hos 12:3 and Hos 12:4 Jacob contends with God, and in Hos 12:4 with the angel; in Gen 32:28 also with men.

parts.grounds: you have striven with God and with men

findings.text: In Gen 32:28 and Hos 12:4 the contending is followed by prevailing; in Gen 32:28 it is the reason for the name Israel, and in Hos 12:4 Jacob then wept and sought favor.

parts.grounds: he wept and sought his favor

findings.text: In Ecclesiastes the speaker looks over what is done under the sun, his own toil and knowing and the work of others, and names each a striving after wind (Ecc 1:14, 2:11 and the rest).

parts.grounds: Then I considered all that my hands had done

findings.text: What is called a striving after wind is named in each verse: toil and its works (Ecc 2:11, 4:4, 4:6), knowing wisdom, madness and folly (Ecc 1:17), the sinner's gathering (Ecc 2:26), a following of people (Ecc 4:16), the wandering of the appetite (Ecc 6:9).

parts.grounds: the wandering of the appetite

findings.text: Each verse joins the striving after wind to vanity, Ecc 2:11 adds that nothing is gained, and Ecc 4:16 that those who come later take no joy in the one followed.

parts.grounds: vanity and a striving after wind

findings.text: Ecc 4:4 names a man's envy of his neighbor as the source of the toil and skill called a striving after wind; Ecc 2:17 sets it with hating life, and the passage runs on to despair (Ecc 2:18-20).

parts.grounds: envy of his neighbor

findings.text: In Ecc 4:6 and Ecc 6:9 'better' sets the striving after wind on the lesser side of a comparison: below a handful of quietness, and with the wandering appetite below the sight of the eyes.

parts.grounds: Better is a handful of quietness

findings.text: In Ecc 1:17 the speaker applied his heart to know wisdom, madness and folly, and perceived that this knowing too was a striving after wind.

parts.grounds: I applied my heart to know wisdom

findings.text: In Ecc 2:26 God gives wisdom, knowledge and joy to the one who pleases him, and to the sinner the business of gathering, which is called a striving after wind.

parts.grounds: God has given wisdom and knowledge and joy
